In 1954, Marion Keech, a housewife, claimed that she received messages from aliens warning of an Armageddon: on December 21st that year, a flood would rise from the Atlantic and wipe out civilization. [[1]] She forwarded the messages to a doctor specializing in alien research, who further transmitted the news.
A cult was soon formed by like-minded people, known as the “Seekers,” who left their family, quit their jobs, gathered and waited for the arrival of a UFO that would save them from doom. As December 22nd dawned, and the world remained the same, not one of the Seekers questioned Keech and the doctor. [[2]] The apparent real-world disproof of their belief paradoxically strengthened the cult.
Leon Festinger and his coauthors studied this phenomenon and in 1956 presented it in When Prophecy Fails, a book on social psychology. [[3]] They focused on cognitive dissonance between the members’ beliefs and actual events. Cognitive dissonance refers to the perception of contradictory information, and the mental toll of it. This often manifests when a person participates in an action that goes against one or more of those things: mainstream feelings, ideas, beliefs, values, and things in the environment.
Many of Festinger’s findings still ring true when we, half a century later, study the cases of fraud victims or cult victims who, despite the apparent risk of being deceived or even after being deceived, stubbornly deny the existence of said deceit. [[4]] While some would accept the fact, others choose to ignore it or vilify those championing the fact, regarding the latter as bad or evil. However, doing either cannot erase the conflict now brewing in their mind. Stressed, they need to “blind” themselves effectively, turning a deaf ear to reason.

options_bank.A: One of the first published cases of dissonance was reported in this book.
options_bank.B: All would perish, except those who believed in a deity called Sanander.
options_bank.C: People feel anxious when their belief contradicts with an established theory or fact.
options_bank.D: Rather, they believed their strong faith had moved and swayed God from imposing such catastrophe on mankind.
options_bank.E: They were particularly intrigued by the Seekers’ coping mechanism in response to the unfulfilled prophecy.

tags.topic: a 1950s doomsday cult and Festinger’s theory of cognitive dissonance
